blocks.text: In 1848 a railway foreman, Phineas Gage, survived an iron tamping rod passing through the front of his skull. He walked, spoke and remembered normally, but friends said he was 'no longer Gage': impulsive, profane and unable to plan. That a hole in one lobe changed character while leaving movement and speech intact is the key idea of this lesson: cortex is organised into regions with distinct jobs.

blocks.markdown: Each cerebral hemisphere is divided into four main lobes. The **central sulcus** separates the **frontal** from the **parietal** lobe, the **lateral sulcus** separates the temporal lobe from the frontal and parietal lobes, and the **parieto-occipital sulcus** separates parietal from **occipital**. Within each lobe, **primary** areas receive sensory input or give motor output, **association** areas integrate it, and in most people the **dominant hemisphere** (the left in over 90% of right-handers and a majority of left-handers) is specialised for language.

**Primary motor cortex (M1)** lies in the **precentral gyrus** (Brodmann area 4) of the frontal lobe. **Primary somatosensory cortex (S1)** lies in the **postcentral gyrus** (areas 3, 1, 2) of the parietal lobe. Both are organised as a distorted map of the contralateral body, the **homunculus**: the **leg and foot** are represented on the **medial** surface (paracentral lobule), then the trunk, arm and **hand** on the dorsolateral convexity, and the **face, lips and tongue** most laterally and inferiorly. The size of each representation depends on **density of innervation**, not physical size: the hands, lips and tongue occupy a large area because they require fine motor control and have many sensory receptors.

blocks.title: A march of seizure activity along the precentral gyrus
blocks.prompt: A 33-year-old man has focal seizures that begin with twitching of the left thumb, spread to the left hand, arm and then the left side of the face, and stop without loss of consciousness. Where is the irritative focus and what does the pattern show?

steps.text: Twitching of the left side means the right hemisphere is involved, because motor cortex controls the contralateral body.
The thumb and hand area is on the dorsolateral convexity of the precentral gyrus; the face lies below it. A seizure spreading from thumb to hand to arm to face moves in the order of the homunculus.
The activity is therefore spreading along the right precentral gyrus.

blocks.answer: A focus in the lateral right precentral gyrus (the hand area), with spread along the motor homunculus (a Jacksonian march).

rows: Motor cortex (M1), premotor cortex, Broca area, prefrontal executive functions and personality
Contralateral weakness; expressive aphasia (dominant); disinhibition, apathy, impaired planning
Somatosensory cortex (S1), sensory association, spatial awareness
Contralateral sensory loss; neglect (non-dominant); inability to recognise objects by touch; Gerstmann syndrome (dominant)
Auditory cortex, Wernicke area, memory (hippocampus, medial temporal)
Receptive aphasia (dominant); memory impairment; contralateral superior quadrantanopia

blocks.title: Broca and Wernicke areas
blocks.text: Broca area lies in the inferior frontal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere (Brodmann areas 44 and 45) and organises the production of speech. Wernicke area lies in the posterior part of the superior temporal gyrus (area 22) and is needed for understanding language. They are linked by the arcuate fasciculus.

blocks.markdown: **Aphasia** is an acquired disorder of language. In **Broca (expressive) aphasia** the speech is effortful, halting and telegraphic with few small words, but **comprehension is relatively preserved** and the patient is often frustrated and aware. Nearby motor cortex involvement often causes a contralateral face and arm weakness. In **Wernicke (receptive) aphasia** the speech is **fluent**, with normal rhythm and grammar-like structure but substitution of wrong words or invented words (paraphasias), and **comprehension is poor**; the patient is usually unaware. In **conduction aphasia**, damage to the arcuate fasciculus disconnects the two areas: speech is fluent and comprehension good, but **repetition is poor**. **Global aphasia** involves both areas.

blocks.title: Interpreting a speech sample
blocks.prompt: A 64-year-old right-handed man says, in a rapid fluent stream, 'The wibbet went to the garp with the things'. He cannot follow the instruction 'touch your nose'. Which area and artery are most likely involved?

steps.text: Speech is fluent but contains wrong or invented words, and he cannot understand a simple command, so comprehension is impaired.
Fluent speech with impaired comprehension is Wernicke aphasia, caused by damage to the posterior superior temporal gyrus of the dominant (left) hemisphere.
That area is in the territory of the inferior division of the left middle cerebral artery (cortical branches).

blocks.answer: Left posterior superior temporal gyrus (Wernicke area): Wernicke receptive aphasia.

items: Frontal lobe: contralateral weakness (precentral), expressive aphasia (inferior frontal, dominant), personality and executive change (prefrontal).
Parietal lobe: contralateral sensory loss; non-dominant lesions cause hemispatial neglect.
Temporal lobe: receptive aphasia (dominant); memory loss (medial temporal); upper quadrant visual field loss from the optic radiation loop.
Occipital lobe: contralateral homonymous hemianopia with no motor or sensory loss.

blocks.title: Do not forget handedness
blocks.text: Language dominance is not the same as handedness. Almost all right-handed people have language in the left hemisphere; most, but not all, left-handers do too. State the dominant side explicitly when localising a language deficit.

points: The primary motor cortex is in the precentral gyrus and the primary somatosensory cortex in the postcentral gyrus; the homunculus has the leg medially and the face and hand laterally, with size proportional to innervation density.
Broca area (inferior frontal gyrus) produces speech, Wernicke area (posterior superior temporal gyrus) mediates comprehension, and the arcuate fasciculus links them.
Lesions of each lobe produce characteristic contralateral deficits: frontal (weakness, personality), parietal (sensory loss, neglect), temporal (language, memory) and occipital (hemianopia).

questions.stem: In which gyrus is the primary somatosensory cortex located?

distractorRationale.a: The precentral gyrus holds the primary motor cortex.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: S1 lies in the parietal lobe behind the central sulcus.
distractorRationale.c: The superior temporal gyrus contains the auditory cortex and Wernicke area.
distractorRationale.d: The cingulate gyrus is part of the limbic system.

questions.explanation: The postcentral gyrus, immediately posterior to the central sulcus, receives somatosensory input from the contralateral body via the thalamus.

questions.stem: Why do the lips and hands occupy a disproportionately large area of the primary somatosensory cortex?

options.text: They are physically the largest body parts
They have a high density of sensory receptors and fine discriminative function
They are supplied by the largest cerebral artery
They lie closest to the central sulcus

questions.correctOptionText: They have a high density of sensory receptors and fine discriminative function

distractorRationale.a: Representation does not reflect physical size.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: cortical area is proportional to innervation density and function.
distractorRationale.c: Blood supply does not determine map size.

questions.explanation: The homunculus is distorted because cortical territory is allocated according to the density of receptors and the precision of sensation or movement. The lips and hands are very densely innervated.

questions.stem: A parasagittal meningioma compresses the medial surface of the left precentral gyrus. Which deficit is most likely?

options.text: Weakness of the right leg and foot
Weakness of the left leg and foot

questions.correctOptionText: Weakness of the right leg and foot

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the leg area is medial and controls the contralateral limb.
distractorRationale.b: The face is lateral, and the left motor cortex controls the right side.
distractorRationale.c: The left cortex controls the right leg.
distractorRationale.d: Broca area is on the lateral surface of the inferior frontal gyrus.

questions.explanation: The medial precentral gyrus (paracentral lobule) contains the leg area. Because the corticospinal tract crosses, a left-sided lesion weakens the right leg.

questions.stem: Where is Broca area located in a right-handed person?

options.text: Inferior frontal gyrus of the left hemisphere
Posterior superior temporal gyrus of the left hemisphere
Inferior frontal gyrus of the right hemisphere
Occipital pole of the left hemisphere

questions.correctOptionText: Inferior frontal gyrus of the left hemisphere

distractorRationale.a: Correct: Broca area is in the dominant inferior frontal gyrus (areas 44, 45).
distractorRationale.c: The right hemisphere is non-dominant for language in most right-handed people.
distractorRationale.d: The occipital pole contains visual cortex.

questions.explanation: Broca area is in the inferior frontal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere, which is the left in nearly all right-handed people. It organises speech production.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old right-handed woman after a stroke speaks fluently with normal rhythm but uses many wrong words, and she cannot follow simple spoken commands. Where is the lesion most likely?

distractorRationale.a: A left inferior frontal lesion would impair production, with comprehension preserved.
distractorRationale.b: An arcuate fasciculus lesion alone would spare comprehension.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: fluent speech with poor comprehension indicates Wernicke area.

questions.explanation: Fluent, paraphasic speech with impaired comprehension is receptive (Wernicke) aphasia. The causative lesion is in the dominant posterior superior temporal gyrus.

questions.stem: True or false: in Broca aphasia, comprehension of spoken language is relatively preserved.
questions.explanation: Broca aphasia is a disorder of speech production: output is effortful and non-fluent, but understanding is relatively intact. Receptive aphasia is the one with impaired comprehension.

questions.stem: A patient after a stroke understands speech and speaks fluently, but cannot repeat the phrase 'no ifs, ands or buts'. Which structure is most likely damaged?

options.text: Primary motor cortex of the face

distractorRationale.c: Correct: disconnection of the two language areas impairs repetition alone (conduction aphasia).
distractorRationale.d: This would cause dysarthria, not an isolated repetition deficit.

questions.explanation: Fluent speech and good comprehension show that Broca and Wernicke areas are intact, so the isolated loss of repetition points to the pathway connecting them, the arcuate fasciculus.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old right-handed man has a stroke affecting the right parietal lobe. He ignores the left half of his body and the left side of the room. What is this called?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: non-dominant parietal damage causes contralateral neglect.
distractorRationale.b: Aphasia is a dominant hemisphere deficit.
distractorRationale.c: Prosopagnosia is a visual recognition disorder.
distractorRationale.d: Dysarthria is a motor speech problem.

questions.explanation: The non-dominant parietal cortex is important for attention to space. A lesion there leads to neglect of the contralateral (left) side, despite intact primary sensation.

questions.stem: Predict one characteristic deficit for a lesion of each of the following lobes: frontal (prefrontal), parietal (non-dominant), temporal (dominant, posterior) and occipital. Give the side affected where applicable.
markingGuide: Prefrontal: personality change, disinhibition or apathy, impaired planning and executive function
Non-dominant parietal: contralateral hemispatial neglect (and contralateral sensory loss)
Contralateral nature of deficits is stated where relevant
questions.explanation: Each lobe contains regions of specialised function, so damage produces a recognisable deficit. Sensory and motor deficits are contralateral because of the crossing of pathways.

questions.stem: Describe the location of the primary motor and primary somatosensory cortices and the layout of the homunculus, and explain why the hand and face areas are large.
markingGuide: Primary motor cortex in the precentral gyrus of the frontal lobe
Primary somatosensory cortex in the postcentral gyrus of the parietal lobe
Leg and foot on the medial surface, trunk, arm and hand on the convexity, face, lips and tongue laterally
Representation is of the contralateral body
Area is proportional to density of innervation and fineness of control, so hand, lips and tongue are large
questions.explanation: Both cortices are strips on either side of the central sulcus with the body mapped from medial (leg) to lateral (face). The distortion reflects the density of motor control and sensory receptors, not physical size.
